{{short description|Type of shift space studied in ergodic theory}}

In [[mathematics]], '''subshifts of finite type''' are [[shift space]]s defined by a finite set of forbidden words. They are used to model [[dynamical systems]], and in particular are objects of study in [[symbolic dynamics]] and [[ergodic theory]]. They also describe the set of all possible sequences executed by a [[finite-state machine]]. The most widely studied [[shift space]]s are the subshifts of finite type.

== Motivating examples ==
One example of a (one-sided) shift of finite type is the set of all sequences, infinite on one end only, that can be made up of the letters <math>A, B</math>, like <math>AAA\cdots, ABAB\cdots, \dots</math>. This is known as a [[shift space#Examples|full shift]] and is denoted by <math>\{A,B\}^\mathbb{N}</math>.

By forbidding the word <math>BB</math>, one defines a shift of finite type <math>\Sigma = \{(x_0,x_1,x_2,\ldots) \mid x_ix_{i+1} \neq BB\}</math> called the [[golden shift]], so-called because the numbers of legal words of length <math>n</math> are the [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci numbers]]. Two-sided shifts of finite type are similar, but consist of sequences that are infinite on both ends.

A subshift can be defined by a directed graph on the letters, such as the graph <math>A \to B \to C \to A</math>. It consists of sequences whose transitions between consecutive letters are only those allowed by the graph. For this example, the subshift consists of only three one-sided sequences: <math>ABCABC\cdots, BCABCA\cdots, CABCAB\cdots</math>. Similarly, the two-sided subshift described by this graph consists of only three two-sided sequences.

Other directed graphs on the same letters produce other subshifts. For example, adding another arrow <math>A\to C</math> to the graph produces a subshift that, instead of containing three sequences, contains [[Cardinality of the continuum|an uncountably infinite number]] of sequences. Up to a local recoding of letters, every subshift of finite type can be described by such a directed graph.

== Definition ==
Let <math>\mathcal{A}</math> be a finite set of <math>n</math> symbols (alphabet).  Let <math>X</math> denote the set <math>\mathcal{A}^\mathbb{Z}</math> of all bi-infinite sequences of elements of <math>\mathcal{A}</math> together with the [[shift operator]] <math>T</math>.  We endow <math>\mathcal{A}</math> with the [[discrete topology]] and <math>X</math> with the [[product topology]].  A '''symbolic flow''' or '''subshift''' is a [[closed set|closed]] <math>T</math>-invariant subset <math>Y</math> of <math>X</math> <ref name="X21">Xie (1996) p.21</ref> and the associated language <math>\mathcal{L}_Y</math> is the set of finite subwords of elements of <math>Y</math>.<ref name="X22">Xie (1996) p.22</ref>

Let <math>F</math> be a finite set of words in the alphabet <math>\mathcal{A}</math>, which are called '''forbidden words'''. The associated '''subshift of finite type''' is defined to be the space

<math display=block>\Sigma_F = \{(x_0,x_1,x_2,\ldots) \mid \forall i,k \geq 0, x_ix_{i+1}\cdots x_{i+k} \notin F\}</math>

of sequences that avoid the set of forbidden words <math>F</math>.

If the sequence extends to infinity in only one direction as above, it is called a '''one-sided''' subshift of finite type, and if it is [[bi-infinite sequence|bilateral]], it is called a '''two-sided''' subshift of finite type.

The [[shift operator]] <math>T</math> maps a sequence in the one- or two-sided shift to another by shifting all symbols to the left, i.e.

<math display=block>(T(x))_{i}=x_{i+1}.</math>

Clearly this map is only invertible in the case of the two-sided shift.

A particularly useful subclass is given by the '''edge shifts'''. Let {{mvar|A}} be an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} [[adjacency matrix]] with entries in {{math|{0, 1}.}} Using these elements we construct a [[directed graph]] {{math|1=''G'' = (''V'', ''E'')}} with {{mvar|V}} the set of vertices and {{mvar|E}} the set of edges containing the directed edge {{math|''x'' → ''y''}} in {{mvar|E}} if and only if {{math|1=''A''{{sub|''x'', ''y''}} = 1}}.  Let {{mvar|Y}} be the set of all infinite '''admissible''' sequences of edges, where by ''admissible'' it is meant that the sequence is a [[Walk (graph theory)|walk]] of the graph, and the sequence can be either one-sided or two-sided infinite.  Let {{mvar|T}} be the [[Shift operator#Sequences|left shift operator]] on such sequences; it plays the role of the time-evolution operator of the dynamical system.  An '''edge shift''' is then defined as a pair {{math|(''Y'', ''T'')}} obtained in this way.

Formally, one may define the sequences of edges as

:<math>\Sigma_{A}^{+} = \left\{ (x_0,x_1,\ldots):
x_j \in V,  A_{x_{j}x_{j+1}}=1, j \in \N \right\}.</math>

This is the space of all sequences of symbols such that the symbol {{mvar|p}} can be followed by the symbol {{mvar|q}} only if the {{math|(''p'', ''q'')}}-th entry of the matrix {{mvar|A}} is 1. The space of all [[bi-infinite sequence]]s is defined analogously:

:<math>\Sigma_{A} = \left\{ (\ldots, x_{-1},x_0,x_1,\ldots):
x_j \in V, A_{x_{j}x_{j+1}}=1, j\in\mathbb{Z} \right\}.</math>

Edge shifts are a subset of the subshifts of finite type whose set of forbidden words comprise only two-letter words. On the other hand, it can be shown that every subshift of finite type is [[Topological conjugacy|topologically conjugate]] to an edge shift via a [[Curtis-Hedlund-Lyndon theorem|local recoding]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lind |first1=Douglas A. |last2=Marcus |first2=Brian |title=An introduction to symbolic dynamics and coding |date=1995 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=9780511626302}}</ref>

An edge shift is called '''transitive''' if {{mvar|G}} is [[Strongly-connected digraph|strongly connected]]: there is a sequence of edges from any one vertex to any other vertex. Subshifts of finite type with dense orbits are precisely those that are conjugate to a transitive edge shift.

An important special case is the '''full {{mvar|n}}-shift''': it has a graph with an edge that connects every vertex to every other vertex; that is, all of the entries of the adjacency matrix are 1.  The full {{mvar|n}}-shift corresponds to the [[Bernoulli scheme]] without the [[measure (mathematics)|measure]].

== Terminology ==

By convention, the term '''shift''' is understood to refer to the full {{mvar|n}}-shift.  A '''subshift''' is then any subspace of the full shift that is shift-invariant (that is, a subspace that is invariant under the action of the shift operator), non-empty, and closed for the product topology defined below. Some subshifts can be characterized by a transition matrix, as above; such subshifts are then called subshifts of finite type.  Often, subshifts of finite type are called simply '''shifts of finite type'''. Subshifts of finite type are also sometimes called '''topological Markov shifts'''.

== Examples ==
Many chaotic [[dynamical system]]s are isomorphic to subshifts of finite type; examples include systems with [[homoclinic connection|transverse homoclinic connections]], [[diffeomorphism]]s of [[closed manifold]]s with positive [[metric entropy]], and piecewise-linear Markov maps of the interval.

==Topology==
A subshift has a natural topology, derived from the [[product topology]] on {{tmath|V^\Z,}} where

:<math>V^\Z= \prod_{n \in \Z} V = \{ x=(\ldots,x_{-1},x_0,x_1,\ldots) : 
x_k \in V \; \forall k \in \Z \}</math>

and {{mvar|V}} is given the [[discrete topology]]. 
A basis for the topology of {{tmath|V^\Z,}} which induces the topology of the subshift, is the family of [[cylinder set]]s

:<math>C_t[a_0, \ldots, a_s]= \{x \in V^\Z :
x_t = a_0, \ldots ,x_{t+s} = a_s \}</math>

The cylinder sets are [[clopen set]]s in {{tmath|V^\Z.}} Every open set in {{tmath|V^\Z}} is a [[countable]] union of cylinder sets. Every open set in the subshift is the intersection of an open set of {{tmath|V^\Z}} with the subshift. With respect to this topology, the shift {{mvar|T}} is a [[homeomorphism]]; that is,  with respect to this topology, it is [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] with continuous inverse.

The space {{tmath|V^\Z}} is homeomorphic to a [[Cantor set]].

==Metric==
A variety of different metrics can be defined on a shift space. One can define a metric on a shift space by considering two points to be "close" if they have many initial symbols in common; this is the [[p-adic metric|{{mvar|p}}-adic metric]]. In fact, both the one- and two-sided shift spaces are [[compact space|compact]] [[metric space]]s.

==Measure==
A subshift of finite type may be endowed with any one of several different [[measure (mathematics)|measures]], thus leading to a [[measure-preserving dynamical system]]. A common object of study is the '''Markov measure''', which is an extension of a [[Markov chain]] to the topology of the shift.

A Markov chain is a pair {{math|(''P'', π)}} consisting of the '''transition matrix''', an {{math|''n'' × ''n''}} matrix {{math|1=''P'' = (''p{{sub|ij}}'')}} for which all {{math|1=''p{{sub|ij}}'' &ge; 0}} and

:<math>\sum_{j=1}^np_{ij}=1</math>

for all {{mvar|i}}. The '''stationary probability vector''' {{math|1=''&pi;'' = (''&pi;{{sub|i}}'')}} has all {{math|1=''&pi;{{sub|i}}'' &ge; 0}}, <math display=inline>\sum \pi_i = 1</math> and has

:<math>\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_i p_{ij}= \pi_j.</math>

A Markov chain, as defined above, is said to be '''compatible''' with the shift of finite type if {{math|1=''p{{sub|ij}}'' = 0}} whenever {{math|1=''A{{sub|ij}}'' = 0}}.  The '''Markov measure''' of a cylinder set may then be defined by

:<math>\mu(C_t[a_0,\ldots,a_s]) = \pi_{a_0} p_{a_0,a_1} \cdots p_{a_{s-1}, a_s}</math>

The [[Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy]] with relation to the Markov measure is

:<math>s_\mu = -\sum_{i=1}^n \pi_i \sum_{j=1}^n p_{ij} \log p_{ij}</math>

=== Markov and non-Markov measures ===
[[File:Blackwell HMM example.png|thumb|193x193px|The hidden part of a hidden Markov model, whose observable states is non-Markovian]]
As above, given a [[Markov transition matrix]] and an invariant distribution on the states, we can impose a [[probability measure]] on the subshift. For example, consider the Markov chain given on the left on the states <math>A, B_1, B_2  </math>, with invariant distribution <math>\pi = (2/7, 4/7, 1/7)   </math>. If we "forget" the distinction between <math>B_1, B_2</math>, we project this subshift on <math>A, B_1, B_2  </math> onto a subshift on <math>A, B</math>, and this projection also projects the probability measure down to a probability measure on the subshift on <math>A, B</math>.

The curious thing is that the probability measure on the subshift on <math>A, B  </math> is not created by a Markov chain on <math>A, B  </math>, not even multiple orders. Intuitively, this is because if one observes a long sequence of <math>B^n</math>, then one would become increasingly sure that the <math>Pr(A | B^n) \to \frac 23   </math>, meaning that the observable part of the system can be affected by something infinitely in the past.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Citation |last1=Boyle |first1=Mike |title=Hidden Markov processes in the context of symbolic dynamics |date=2010-01-13 |last2=Petersen |first2=Karl|arxiv=0907.1858 }}</ref>

Conversely, there exists a subshift on 6 symbols, projected to a subshift on 2 symbols, such that any Markov measure on the smaller subshift has a preimage measure that is not Markov of any order (Example 2.6 <ref name=":1" />).

==Zeta function==
The [[Artin–Mazur zeta function]] is defined as the [[formal power series]]

:<math>\zeta(z)=\exp\left(\sum_{n=1}^\infty \Bigl| \textrm{Fix} (T^n) \Bigr| \frac {z^n}{n}\right),</math>

where {{math|Fix(''T<sup> n</sup>'')}} is the set of [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]s of the {{mvar|n}}-fold shift.<ref name=BS60/>   It has a product formula

:<math>\zeta(z) = \prod_\gamma \left(1-z^{|\gamma|} \right)^{-1} \ </math>

where {{mvar|γ}} runs over the closed orbits.<ref name=BS60>Brin & Stuck (2002) p.60</ref>  For subshifts of finite type, the zeta function is a [[rational function]] of {{mvar|z}}:<ref name=BS61>Brin & Stuck (2002) p.61</ref>

:<math>\zeta(z) = (\det(I-zA))^{-1} \ . </math>

== Generalizations ==
A '''sofic shift''' is an image of a subshift of finite type where different edges of the transition graph may be mapped to the same symbol. For example, if one only watches the output from a hidden Markov chain, then the output appears to be a sofic system.<ref name=":0">''[https://web.archive.org/web/20221005013617/https://petersen.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/17054/2018/04/Main.pdf Sofic Measures: Characterizations of Hidden Markov Chains by Linear Algebra, Formal Languages, and Symbolic Dynamics]'' - Karl Petersen, Mathematics 210, Spring 2006, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill</ref> It may be regarded as the set of labellings of paths through an [[Automata theory|automaton]]: a subshift of finite type then corresponds to an automaton which is [[Deterministic automaton|deterministic]].<ref name=PF205>Pytheas Fogg (2002) p.205</ref> Such systems correspond to [[regular language]]s.

Context-free systems are defined analogously, and are generated by [[phrase structure grammar]]s.

A '''renewal system''' is defined to be the set of all infinite concatenations of some fixed finite collection of finite words.

Subshifts of finite type are identical to free (non-interacting) one-dimensional [[Potts model]]s ({{mvar|n}}-letter generalizations of [[Ising model]]s),  with certain nearest-neighbor configurations excluded. Interacting Ising models are defined as subshifts together with a continuous function of the configuration space{{definition|date=April 2019}} (continuous with respect to the product topology, defined below); the [[partition function (mathematics)|partition function]] and [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] are explicitly expressible in terms of this function.{{clarify|reason=Is this a requirement or a result?|date=April 2019}}

Subshifts may be quantized in a certain way, leading to the idea of the [[quantum finite automata]].
